cells.tense: You have something in your hands right now, and you already know it is worth carrying.
cells.ask: Pick the one piece of the shared thing you would hand someone first, and give it to them this week — in your own words, not the form you inherited.
cells.core:
You have hold of something worth keeping, and you are not gripping it too hard. A practice, a way of explaining, a story that came down to you — you carry it in a way that leaves room for the people you are passing it to. That is why it keeps living: you hold the shape without closing your hand around it. The room you share with others is a little steadier where you stand.

The thing to watch is that holding can turn into hoarding without a sound. A shared thing grows on being handed over. So this week, offer one piece of it to a person who would use it — plainly, in the words you would actually say, in a way they can take and put down. What you keep after you have given it is the proof it was yours to give.
cells.sheetLine: You carry something worth keeping, and your hands stay open.

cells.tense: You are already bracing to defend the thing in your hands before anyone has come for it.
cells.ask: Once today, let a question about the thing you are carrying land without answering it in the same breath. Sit with what they said. The point is to let their version stand beside yours for a minute, not to give anything up.
cells.core:
You are guarding something you have not planted yet. There is a version of this shared thing that is already fully preserved and agreed-upon, and you are pushing toward it — explaining, insisting, making sure the people around you hold it the way you do. The certainty is spending the very thing it is protecting: conversation you were part of turns into a case you are making, and the shared part of it slips away.

Ease off the grip and something real can come back: the thing is not a fortress. It lives because people can feel their way into it. So let one question stand unanswered for a while, without a correction riding in behind it. This is not loosening what matters. It is letting it breathe long enough to hold other people again.

cells.tense: You keep the thing you carry close and private, and you have not put any of it into another person's hands.
cells.ask: Choose one practice or piece of what you carry and teach it to one person, from scratch, as if you were both new to it. Ten minutes, no audience, no standard to meet. You are only showing someone the rope.
cells.core:
The thing itself is intact. You still know it, and it still moves you when you are alone with it. What has gone quiet is handing any of it to another person. You keep it close, and you keep it private, and the two have started to look the same. Where you go, it goes, but it does not reach anyone else.

That is loneliness you probably call being practical. So give yourself a beginning you cannot fail at: teach a small piece to someone who has no reason to judge it, in your own words, and let the first version be rough. The aim is not the lesson. The aim is to find out whether the thing still wants to move through you, and to let one other person be in the room when it does.
cells.sheetLine: The thing is still yours. What is missing is passing it on.

cells.tense: You are already the one deciding what gets passed on around you, and you keep calling it just how things are.
cells.ask: Name one thing you have shaped about what your group or family carries — the way something is done, said, or explained — and say plainly that you are the one who made it that way. Just to yourself, or to the person next to you.
cells.core:
The way something is done where you are did not arrive by itself. Someone decided the wording, the order, the version worth repeating — and that someone has been you, more often than you have admitted. People around you already take the shape you give this shared thing; it is shaping what they think is normal.

What you have not done is say so. Not to claim credit — credit is the wrong frame. Owning it is what makes it available for care: you can only tend a thing you admit you made. So name it once, simply, without improving the story. The older, plainer version of this — before it turned into a pattern — is where you pick the line back up, pen in your own hand.
cells.sheetLine: You have been writing this already. Say that it is yours.
